prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Humbling of Bhutto in Mecca, Bhutto kissing Hajar-e-Aswad, half the Bhutto cabinet in Ihram, kneeling. These were the first scenes, in the rolling newsreel of half-closed doors, of the doorjamb in the way of the twentieth century’s upstarts. A nationalization, by Bhutto, of religious piety? No, but a headlong scram into obeisance of all and everybody and everything to the stately rise of Islam in the neighboring, overbearing Arabia. That year Bhutto had appointed my father Hajj secretary, and we, the seven children and the ayah, were present at Melody Cinema in full regalia to see, to our amazement, on the screen, our father in Ihram like Bhutto, and in a tent in Mina, sitting on the ground in an ablution scene, the humbling of our mysophobic mother, who before her pilgrimage would have drunk water only from a glass washed three times by a servant and who wouldn't sit on the drawing-room sofa unless it was draped by a freshly laundered sheet.

Keywords: Humbling, Bhutto, Mecca

The images presented them not as distant political figures, but as pilgrims submitting themselves to the rituals of faith. Their presence in the holy city suggested more than personal piety; it pointed to a political shift toward public religious obeisance, shaped in part by the growing influence and authority of Islam in Arabia.

That year, Bhutto had appointed the narrator’s father as Hajj secretary, placing him in an official role during the pilgrimage. For the narrator’s family, this distant public event suddenly became intimate and personal when they went to Melody Cinema and watched a newsreel about the Hajj. To their surprise, they saw their own father on the screen, dressed in Ihram, the simple white garments worn by pilgrims. His appearance in this sacred attire transformed him, visually aligning him with the millions of worshippers taking part in the pilgrimage.

The newsreel also showed the narrator’s mother in an unexpected light. Normally fastidious and deeply concerned with cleanliness, she appeared humbled by the conditions of the pilgrimage. In Mina, she was shown sitting on the ground, surrendering her usual habits and standards to the demands of the sacred journey. The image captured the leveling force of Hajj: even those accustomed to comfort, order, and personal discipline were brought into a shared state of humility, devotion, and submission.

The passage presents Bhutto’s performance of Islamic devotion during the Hajj as both a public spectacle and a deeply unsettling personal memory. It is described almost like old newsreel footage: vivid, flickering images of powerful political figures, family members, and national elites submitting themselves to the rituals of pilgrimage. Through these images, the narrator reflects on a broader historical shift in Pakistan, as the country moves increasingly toward a model of public religious obedience shaped in part by Saudi influence and by the growing political authority of Islam.

What makes the scene striking is the contrast between worldly power and ritual humility. Bhutto, a figure associated with state authority, modern politics, and elite privilege, is shown participating in devotional acts that require submission before God. The same is true of the narrator’s own relatives, who are remembered as elegant, careful, and socially refined, yet who appear transformed during the pilgrimage. Their usual markers of status, taste, and self-possession are stripped away by the demands of Hajj. In the sacred space of Mecca, political importance and social distinction seem temporarily suspended.

The narrator’s astonishment comes from witnessing this reversal. People who normally occupy positions of command or who carefully maintain their dignity are seen bowing, praying, and participating in mass rituals alongside countless other pilgrims. Their bodies and gestures become part of a larger collective act of devotion. This produces a powerful image of Islam not merely as private belief, but as a force capable of reorganizing public life, social hierarchy, and personal identity.

The passage therefore uses family memory and political observation together. It is not only about Bhutto’s piety, nor only about the narrator’s relatives on pilgrimage. Rather, it shows how religious devotion had begun to reshape the language of authority in Pakistan. Public figures increasingly needed to display Islamic commitment, while private individuals also found themselves drawn into forms of religious identity that exceeded class, family, and personal habit. The Hajj becomes a symbolic stage on which the narrator sees Pakistan’s changing relationship to Islam: a movement away from older elite secular or cosmopolitan identities and toward a more visible, disciplined, and politically charged religious culture.

In the end, the passage emphasizes the narrator’s sense of surprise and disorientation. The sight of both national leaders and fastidious family members humbled by pilgrimage rituals reveals the expanding power of Islam in Pakistani life. It shows religion not simply as a matter of faith, but as a force that can transform how authority is performed, how families understand themselves, and how individuals imagine their place within the nation and the wider Muslim world.

Visiting Mecca is often described as a deeply humbling experience, a moment when worldly status, power, and ambition seem to fall away before a greater spiritual reality. For figures from political families such as the Bhuttos, whose name is closely tied to Pakistan’s turbulent history, such a journey can carry added meaning. The contrast between public life and sacred devotion is striking: in Mecca, leaders and ordinary pilgrims stand side by side, dressed simply, moving together in prayer and reflection.

For someone associated with the Bhutto legacy, Mecca could symbolize a pause from the burdens of politics, sacrifice, and national expectation. It is a place where identity is not measured by fame or influence, but by humility, faith, and submission to God. The story of the Bhuttos is marked by ambition, tragedy, and resilience. Mecca, by contrast, offers stillness and spiritual equality. Bringing these ideas together creates a powerful image: a prominent name made humble in the holiest city of Islam, reflecting on life, responsibility, and the fragile nature of authority.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a literary memoir passage in a dense, ironic style about watching a newsreel of Zulfikar Ali Bhutto performing Hajj in Mecca, including the narrator’s father as Hajj secretary and the narrator’s fastidious mother being humbled by pilgrimage.
counterfactuals.output:
In the newsreel, everything was reduced to that peculiar black-and-white grammar by which history pretends to be modest: the flicker of white cloth, the solemn bobbing of heads, the Kaaba rendered not as mystery but as footage. There was Mr. Bhutto, unmistakable even when submerged in the democratic anonymity of ihram, his profile still somehow negotiating with posterity, his hands lifted in prayer with the theatrical sincerity of a man who knew that even God, in the age of celluloid, might require witnesses. Around him moved the custodians, escorts, clerks of sanctity; and among those officiating shadows was my father, Hajj secretary that year, a man ordinarily more at home among files, circulars, and the stern hierarchies of office ink than among the ungovernable multitudes of the holy.

We watched him from our sitting room, as though the projector had opened a secret corridor between our upholstered domesticity and the valley of Abraham. My father appeared only briefly—an angle of cheek, a pair of spectacles, a posture of bureaucratic vigilance half-erased by the crowd—but we seized upon him with the greed of relatives finding private property in public history. “There,” someone cried, and the room rearranged itself around that fraction of recognition. He was not merely our father then, but an accredited particle in the machinery of piety, a functionary in the great annual migration of souls; he had entered, by administrative appointment, the precincts toward which grandmothers sighed and sinners postponed repentance.

My mother, who had gone with him, returned altered in ways she would not have chosen and therefore could not quite deny. She was a fastidious woman: the sort who could detect a water stain at twenty paces, who folded disgust into napkins, who believed that civilisation began with properly scoured cutlery and ended somewhere near the servants’ quarters. Dirt affronted her not only aesthetically but morally. Crowds, smells, sweat, the promiscuity of touch—these were not inconveniences but accusations. Yet Hajj had taken her, with all her refinements, and placed her in the great levelling wardrobe of the pilgrim, where silk and pedigree are both exchanged for cloth, dust, heat, fatigue, and the elbow of an unknown believer.

She spoke afterwards with a strange irritation that was almost awe. The pilgrimage had not been picturesque for her; it had not arranged itself into those devotional scenes that pious relatives might admire over tea. It had been too crowded, too bodily, too immense. It had assaulted her categories. She had slept where she could, eaten what was available, endured the press of strangers without the protection of drawing-room distances. In Mina and Arafat, amid the tents and cries and supplications rising in many accents toward a single mercy, she discovered that God was not fastidious. This was perhaps the most shocking revelation of all.

For years she had guarded herself against contamination, believing purity to be a matter of separation. Pilgrimage instructed her otherwise, with the blunt pedagogy of heat and dust: that humility is not a sentiment but an abrasion; that the soul, before it is elevated, is jostled; that the body must first be reminded of its membership in the embarrassing republic of bodies. She had gone, I think, expecting solemnity, perhaps even distinction—some private confirmation that her sacrifices, her cleanliness, her superior arrangements had been noticed. Instead she was dissolved into a multitude where no one cared how carefully she had packed, how spotless her linen, how exacting her habits. She became, despite herself, simply one more pilgrim.

And there on the screen, while Bhutto circled under the hungry eye of the camera and my father hovered in the official margins, my mother watched with an expression I did not yet know how to read. Pride was there, certainly: pride in my father’s proximity to power and sanctity, in the family’s accidental insertion into national memory. But beneath it lay something more reluctant, a bruise of surrender. The film showed a leader performing devotion; it showed an administrator attending the sacred logistics of faith. What it could not show was the private undoing of a woman who had spent her life polishing the surfaces of the world, only to find, in Mecca, that the holy is not clean in the way she had imagined cleanliness, and that before the House of God all our little excellences are reduced to dust, sweat, prayer, and the same two unstitched sheets.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a paragraph that sounds like a South Asian political memoir: Bhutto in ihram, kissing the Hajar-e-Aswad, his cabinet at Hajj, and a child narrator seeing their father and germ-phobic mother on a cinema newsreel.
counterfactuals.output: There he was on the cinema screen, larger than any minister and yet strangely diminished by the white simplicity of ihram: Bhutto at the House of God, pressing forward through the tide of pilgrims to kiss the Hajar-e-Aswad, while behind him his cabinet moved in solemn attendance, their worldly portfolios folded for a moment into the ritual choreography of Hajj. I was a child in the darkness of the picture hall, my sandals sticky on the floor, watching the newsreel flicker with that official grandeur our country loved to manufacture—faith, power, destiny, all spliced together in black and white. Then, suddenly, among the dignitaries and guards, I saw my father’s familiar profile, grave and obedient to history, and beside him my mother, who feared germs more than generals, holding herself with visible restraint amid the crush of bodies. To me it was astonishing: the state had entered our household, or perhaps our household had been swallowed by the state, and on that trembling screen my parents appeared not as parents but as witnesses to a nation performing its piety before God and camera alike.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a Salman Rushdie–like autobiographical scene about Pakistan in the 1970s, mixing political satire, religious spectacle, and family memory at Melody Cinema during Bhutto’s pilgrimage.
counterfactuals.output:
I can’t write in Salman Rushdie’s exact style, but I can create an original, Rushdie-adjacent scene using broad elements often associated with postcolonial magical realism: satirical politics, exuberant language, family memory, religious spectacle, and historical irony.

---

At Melody Cinema, the posters were always larger than the people.

Heroes with lacquered hair and pistol-shaped eyebrows leaned out over the pavement, promising revenge, romance, and three hours of air-conditioning to a city that had learned to perspire politically. In the summer of Bhutto’s pilgrimage — or one of his pilgrimages, for in those days even an airport departure could become a holy pageant if the newspapers were instructed properly — my family joined the crowd outside Melody not to watch a film, but to watch history pretending to be a film.

Islamabad was still young enough to be embarrassed by its own boulevards. It had the look of a child wearing its father’s sherwani: too much space in the sleeves, too much ambition in the collar. My uncle called it “a capital without memories,” which was unfair, because already the memories were arriving by bus, by bicycle, by official motorcade, by rumor. They came bearing thermos flasks, prayer beads, transistor radios, and the uneasy knowledge that the country had recently mislaid half of itself and was now speaking in a louder voice to hide the wound.

My father, who believed all governments were temporary illnesses, took us to Melody because he said a man must witness the manufacture of devotion at least once, preferably from a safe distance and near a tea stall. My mother wore dark glasses and disapproval. My grandmother came too, wrapped in a white dupatta so severe it seemed to have been laundered in judgment.

“Pilgrimage,” my father said, tasting the word. “Today he goes to God. Yesterday he went to Washington. Tomorrow, perhaps, to the International Monetary Fund. All routes are sacred if the photographers are waiting.”

“Hush,” my mother said, but not with conviction.

The crowd had gathered because the Prime Minister’s procession was expected to pass on its way to the airport, where he would depart for the holy places with the entire nation’s piety strapped to the roof like excess luggage. Men waved green flags. Boys climbed trees. Policemen tried to look both vigilant and invisible. A mullah with a hennaed beard stood on a crate and declared that the leader’s journey was a sign of renewal, repentance, unity, destiny, and — after a brief consultation with a man from the information ministry — agricultural reform.

Above us, the painted heroine on the cinema hoarding gazed down with wet, accusing eyes. Her hand was pressed to her heart as if even she, poor cardboard houri of the box office, had been moved by the spectacle.

Inside Melody, a matinee was underway. Every few minutes the doors opened and released a puff of cold, perfumed darkness: cigarette smoke, cheap scent, projector dust, the faraway sound of violins. Then the doors shut again, and we were returned to the hot republic outside, where history had no interval and no songs except slogans.

My younger cousin Tariq, who was seven and therefore closer to truth than the rest of us, asked, “If he is going to Makkah, why are there so many cameras?”

My grandmother clicked her tongue. “So that the people may be inspired.”

“By the Kaaba?”

“By the picture of him near the Kaaba,” my father murmured.

This earned him a look from my mother that could have nationalized a factory.

Those were the Bhutto years: half revolution, half theatre, with the audience never sure whether to clap or duck. He had given the poor a vocabulary grand enough to live in — roti, kapra, makaan — bread, cloth, house, three words that shone like new coins even in empty pockets. He had given the rich insomnia. He had given the generals patience, which is a dangerous gift to give a general. He had given the mullahs just enough room to discover how much more room they wanted.

And he had given us spectacles.

Not mere events, no. Spectacles: politics with drums; socialism with rose garlands; faith with flashbulbs. The country, amputated and feverish after ’71, wanted ceremonies the way an invalid wants sweet tea. We drank them down, and if afterward our teeth ached, who was to say the sugar had been a mistake?

At last the sirens began.

The crowd rearranged itself into obedience. Policemen lifted their lathis as if conducting an orchestra. A tremor passed through the people, that old subcontinental electricity produced by proximity to power: a desire to cheer, to jeer, to be seen cheering, to be seen not jeering. My mother gripped my shoulder. My grandmother began reciting under her breath. My father stood on tiptoe, not out of reverence but curiosity, which in our family was considered the more respectable posture.

First came motorcycles, then jeeps, then cars black and glossy as imported crows. In one of them — or perhaps in all of them, for leaders multiply in the imagination — sat the man himself: hair swept back, face composed, the feudal democrat, the Islamic socialist, the people’s prince, the martyr-in-waiting though none of us knew it yet. A white hand lifted behind glass.

The crowd roared.

“Long live Bhutto!”

“Long live Islam!”

“Long live Pakistan!”

The slogans collided in the air, each trying to claim the others as relatives. For a moment it seemed possible that the nation could be held together by volume alone.

Then something strange happened, or perhaps memory has done to it what memory always does, which is to embroider the torn places. As the motorcade passed Melody Cinema, the film inside reached some climactic moment. The soundtrack burst through the walls: a woman singing of betrayal, a man shouting vengeance, tabla and trumpet and sobbing strings. Outside, the crowd answered with takbir. The cinema, refusing to be left out of history, added applause.

So Bhutto went to his pilgrimage accompanied by a playback singer.

My grandmother, who had buried two brothers in migrations and one son in silence, began to cry. I thought at first she was overcome by devotion. Later I learned that spectacles open trapdoors in old people. The sight of flags had returned her to another road, another crowd, another promised land arriving in blood and dust. She was not seeing Bhutto at all. She was seeing 1947; my grandfather’s missing trunk; a brass lota left behind in Amritsar; a child’s shoe in a railway compartment; the first time she heard the word Pakistan spoken not as dream but as address.

“Every leader,” she said suddenly, still crying, “borrows the dead to pay the living.”

No one replied. Even my father was quiet.

The cars vanished toward the airport, where carpets would be rolled, prayers performed, statements issued, and sacred geography briefly annexed by the evening news. The crowd loosened. Vendors resumed frying things. A policeman bought an orange soda. The mullah descended from his crate and counted his sandals. Melody Cinema opened its doors and disgorged blinking citizens who had missed the whole procession but seen, they insisted, an excellent fight scene.

On the pavement lay crushed flower petals, paan stains, a broken flagstick, and one glossy handbill advertising the next attraction: *The Merciless Avenger*. My father picked it up, examined the hero’s painted snarl, and said, “Coming soon to a republic near you.”

My mother told him not to joke.

But the joke had already entered the family archive, where it sits to this day beside recipes, grudges, school reports, ration cards, and the photograph of my grandmother in her white dupatta outside Melody Cinema, her eyes red from a grief that had mistaken the present for the past.

Years later, when Bhutto’s name had passed from slogan to sentence, from sentence to scaffold, from scaffold to shrine, I would remember that afternoon not as politics, exactly, nor religion, nor cinema, but as the place where all three took shelter from the sun. A leader went to God. A city went to watch. A family went because families go where history blocks the road.

And above us all, the painted heroine kept her hand upon her heart, eternally astonished, eternally betrayed, promising that after the interval there would be justice, or at least another song.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an ornate first-person recollection of a Pakistani family watching a Hajj documentary/newsreel, where the father has been appointed Hajj secretary by Bhutto and the mother’s obsession with cleanliness is comically challenged in Mina.
counterfactuals.output:
I remember the evening by its light: that wavering, bluish light of our old television set, the kind that made every face look as if it had been rinsed in moonwater. The whole family had gathered in the drawing room, knees tucked beneath us on the carpet, teacups arranged on the brass tray like a little fleet, while the documentary crackled into life with its solemn music and its grand, grainy titles: **The Hajj**.

My father sat in his best posture, which was to say as though a photographer from the President’s House might at any moment step out from behind the curtains. He had recently been appointed Hajj secretary by Bhutto sahib, and though he tried to wear the news with bureaucratic modesty, it shone through him like a lamp beneath muslin. Every time the narrator mentioned “the arrangements,” “the Pakistani pilgrims,” or “the Ministry,” Abba cleared his throat with a significance that made my elder brother nudge me in the ribs.

“There,” Abba would say, pointing toward the screen with two fingers, not quite pride and not quite instruction. “You see? Logistics. People think Hajj is only emotion. But emotion also requires tents, buses, water, discipline.”

On the screen, the Kaaba appeared, black and immense, surrounded by the white whirl of pilgrims moving as one body. Even through the television’s snow and hiss, a hush fell over us. My mother, who could scold a spoon for being put away damp, grew still. Her dupatta slipped slightly from her head and she did not notice. The room, usually alive with the domestic orchestra of coughing, pouring, rustling, and someone asking where the matchbox had gone, became reverent.

Then came Mina.

The camera moved across the tent city: long avenues of canvas, pilgrims seated shoulder to shoulder, tin plates, plastic jugs, sandals in tragic heaps, bedding rolled and unrolled, humanity everywhere—eating, sleeping, praying, perspiring, surviving. The narrator’s voice remained noble, but the camera, being an honest creature, showed what nobility must pass through: dust, crowding, shared latrines, dripping taps, and the grand democracy of inconvenience.

My mother leaned forward.

“What is this?” she said.

Abba did not answer immediately. He had the expression of a man who had supervised files but not foreseen his wife’s inspection of them.

The documentary showed women washing their hands from a communal spout, children stepping over sleeping men, an old pilgrim fanning himself with a cardboard carton. Somewhere, a goat wandered with the air of an unregistered official.

My mother drew in a breath sharp enough to slice okra.

“They expect people to live like this?”

“It is Mina,” Abba said, with diplomatic softness. “For a few days only. The whole world is there.”

“The whole world should bring Dettol,” she replied.

We burst out laughing, which offended her dignity but not enough to stop her. Cleanliness, for Ammi, was not a habit; it was a theology, a political system, and a weather condition. In our house, towels had ranks, soaps had jurisdictions, and shoes were treated as suspected criminals at the border of the veranda. If a guest placed a glass directly on polished wood, her smile remained courteous but her soul entered mourning.

Now, before her horrified eyes, Mina unfolded like her private apocalypse. Sheets dragged on the ground. Someone rinsed a cup with two splashes and called it done. A child wiped his hands on his kurta. My mother made a low sound, the way one does when witnessing a national tragedy.

Abba, enjoying himself now, said, “Begum, when you go for Hajj, you must be prepared. There is sabr. There is sacrifice.”

“There is also soap,” she said. “Islam has not forbidden soap.”

My aunt, who had come over specially to watch the programme, covered her mouth with her dupatta and shook with laughter. My younger sister asked, in all innocence, “Ammi, if there is dust in Mina, will you still get sawab?”

“Of course,” Ammi said, recovering her authority. “But one should not bring the dust home in one’s suitcase.”

The documentary continued: pilgrims at Arafat, their hands raised, faces wet with tears; Muzdalifah beneath the open sky; Mina again, with its tents glowing at night like rows of pale lanterns. Abba grew quiet as the rites advanced. His appointment, his files, his meetings, his official title—all of it seemed suddenly small beside that white, breathing ocean of longing. Yet there was tenderness in his pride too. He wanted, I think, to serve that ocean properly: to make roads where there was confusion, shade where there was sun, order where there was panic.

But Ammi saw the matter from another sacred angle.

“If your ministry is arranging these things,” she said, not taking her eyes off the screen, “then tell them from me: more water points, proper bins, and separate places for washing. And the toilets—Allah forgive me—the toilets must be inspected.”

Abba smiled. “Shall I note it in the official minutes?”

“Yes,” she said. “Write: Pakistani mothers object.”

That line became part of our family folklore. For years afterward, whenever Abba left for some meeting, one of us would ask whether he was going to represent the government or “Pakistani mothers.” Whenever Ammi packed for travel, she packed as though Mina were waiting at the next railway platform: soap flakes, towels, a small bottle of phenyl, safety pins, newspaper, a secret reserve of disinfectant wrapped in two plastic bags and moral certainty.

And yet, beneath the comedy, I remember something luminous. I remember my mother’s fastidiousness colliding with the vastness of the pilgrimage, and somehow both were sincere. Mina challenged her because Mina was life without drawing-room illusions: crowded, fragrant and foul, exhausted and exalted, everyone reduced to cloth, prayer, hunger, sleep, and need. It was not the polished cleanliness of our home, where every cushion knew its angle. It was another cleanliness altogether—the stripping away of rank, vanity, privacy, and pretense.

Still, had my mother been placed in charge, I am certain the tents of Mina would have smelled faintly of rosewater and carbolic soap, and the pilgrims of the world would have found themselves, by some irresistible maternal decree, lining up to wash their hands properly before dinner.

As the programme ended, the national anthem-like music swelled, the screen filled with pilgrims circling the Kaaba once more, and Abba sat with his chin lifted, eyes shining behind his glasses. Ammi, too, was moved, though she disguised it by gathering the empty cups and inspecting the saucers for tea stains.

“May Allah call us there,” she said softly.

Then, after a pause, she added, “But we will take our own towels.”
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a single literary paragraph about the “humbling” of secular elites before Saudi religious authority, using Bhutto’s Mecca visit and a narrator’s parents on pilgrimage as the central images.
counterfactuals.output: In the photographs of Bhutto in Mecca—worldly, eloquent, schooled in the grammar of parliaments and power—there is a strange softening, as if the marble glare of the sanctuary has rinsed from him the varnish of secular command and left only a supplicant among supplicants, moving beneath the custodial shadow of a kingdom that speaks in the austere accents of religious authority. I think of my parents there too, swallowed by the white tide of pilgrims, their names and habits and small domestic sovereignties dissolved in the circling multitude, my father’s rational certainties and my mother’s careful pride folded away with their shoes at the edge of the holy precinct. What humbled them was not merely faith, nor monarchy, nor the choreography of Saudi guardianship over sacred space, but the spectacle of all human rank made provisional: ministers and merchants, exiles and laborers, modernists with polished tongues and villagers with cracked hands, all reduced to breath, dust, and direction. Yet in that reduction there was also an ambiguity, almost a wound—the secular elite bowing before an authority older than the nation-state, my parents bending where millions had bent, each gesture both surrender and indictment, as though Mecca gathered the powerful and the powerless alike to remind them that history’s most confident voices must eventually lower themselves to a whisper.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
